claim: Transporter research primarily relies on the canonical substrates of well-established transporters.
source: Transporter research primarily relies on the canonical substrates of well-established transporters.

claim: The canonical substrate approach has limitations when studying transporters for low-abundant micromolecules such as micronutrients.
source: This approach has limitations when studying transporters for the low-abundant micromolecules, such as micronutrients, and may not reveal physiological functions of the transporters.

claim: d-serine is a trace enantiomer of serine in the circulation.
source: While d-serine, a trace enantiomer of serine in the circulation, was discovered as an emerging biomarker of kidney function, its transport mechanisms in the periphery remain unknown.

claim: d-serine was discovered as an emerging biomarker of kidney function.

claim: ASCT2 serves as a d-serine transporter previously uncharacterized in the kidney.
source: We revealed that the small amino acid transporter ASCT2 serves as a d-serine transporter previously uncharacterized in the kidney and discovered d-serine as a non-canonical substrate of the sodium-coupled monocarboxylate transporters (SMCTs).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: d-serine is a non-canonical substrate of sodium-coupled monocarboxylate transporters (SMCTs).

claim: ASCT2 and SMCTs are physiologically complementary d-serine transport systems.
source: These two systems are physiologically complementary, but ASCT2 dominates the role in the pathological condition.

claim: ASCT2 dominates d-serine transport in pathological conditions.
source: These two systems are physiologically complementary, but ASCT2 dominates the role in the pathological condition.
evidence: This is a conclusion about ASCT2's role in disease conditions.

claim: d-serine in body fluid was discovered as a promising biomarker for acute kidney injury (AKI).
source: d-Serine in the body fluid was discovered as a promising biomarker for acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) due to its clear association with kidney function in rodents and humans (Sasabe et al., 2014; Kimura et al., 2016; Inoue et al., 2018; Hesaka et al., 2019; Okushima et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about d-serine as a biomarker, supported by citations.

claim: d-serine in body fluid was discovered as a promising biomarker for chronic kidney disease (CKD).

evidence: This is a statement about d-serine as a biomarker, supported by citations.

claim: d-serine has a clear association with kidney function in rodents and humans.

claim: Transport of d-serine has long been found to take place at the proximal tubules.
source: The transport of d-serine has long been found to take place at the proximal tubules (Kragh-Hansen and Sheikh, 1984; Shimomura et al., 1988; Silbernagl et al., 1999; Sasabe and Suzuki, 2019), yet the corresponding transporter has not been clearly elucidated.
evidence: This is a statement about the location of d-serine transport, supported by citations.

claim: The transporter corresponding to d-serine transport at proximal tubules has not been clearly elucidated.

evidence: This is a statement about a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: d-serine is found at submillimolar levels in the brain.
source: d-Serine is found at submillimolar levels in the brain (Hashimoto et al., 1992), where it acts as an obligatory physiological co-agonist of N-methyl-d-aspartate receptors (Mothet et al., 2000; Basu et al., 2009; Papouin et al., 2012; Wolosker, 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about d-serine concentration in the brain, supported by citation.

claim: d-serine acts as an obligatory physiological co-agonist of N-methyl-d-aspartate receptors in the brain.
source: d-Serine is found at submillimolar levels in the brain (Hashimoto et al., 1992), where it acts as an obligatory physiological co-agonist of N-methyl-d-aspartate receptors (Mothet et al., 2000; Basu et al., 2009; Papouin et al., 2012; Wolosker, 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about d-serine's function in the brain, supported by citations.

claim: d-serine in the brain is transported by ASCT1 (SLC1A4).

evidence: This is a statement about d-serine transporters in the brain, supported by citations.

claim: d-serine in the brain is transported by ASCT2 (SLC1A5).
source: Extensive studies of d-serine in the brain show that d-serine is transported by four plasma membrane transporters: ASCT1 (SLC1A4), ASCT2 (SLC1A5), Asc-1 (SLC7A10), and SNAT1 (SLC38A1) (Rosenberg et al., 2013; Foster et al., 2016; Kaplan et al., 2018; Bodner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about d-serine transporters in the brain, supported by citations.

evidence: This is a statement about d-serine transporters in the brain, supported by citations.

claim: d-serine in the brain is transported by SNAT1 (SLC38A1).

claim: Mammals acquire d-serine by biosynthesis via serine racemase function.
source: Mammals acquire d-serine by biosynthesis via serine racemase function (Wolosker et al., 1999) and absorption from the diet and gut microbiota presumably via intestinal transport system(s) (Sasabe and Suzuki, 2019; Inoue et al., 2018; Gonda et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a statement about d-serine biosynthesis, supported by citation.

claim: Mammals acquire d-serine by absorption from the diet and gut microbiota presumably via intestinal transport system(s).
source: Mammals acquire d-serine by biosynthesis via serine racemase function (Wolosker et al., 1999) and absorption from the diet and gut microbiota presumably via intestinal transport system(s) (Sasabe and Suzuki, 2019; Inoue et al., 2018; Gonda et al., 2023).

claim: A d-serine transporter in the intestine is unknown.

claim: The ratios of plasma d-/l-serine were increased in a time-dependent manner from 4 to 40 hr after ischemia-reperfusion.
source: Among amino acids, only the ratios of plasma d-/l-serine were increased in a time-dependent manner from 4 to 40 hr after the ischemia-reperfusion (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the amino acid metabolomics experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The elevation of plasma d-/l-serine ratios at early time points (4 hr–8 hr) was due to a sharp decrease of the l-isomer.
source: The elevation of plasma d-/l-serine ratios at early time points (4 hr–8 hr) was due to a sharp decrease of the l-isomer, while the rise of d-/l-serine ratios at late time points (20 hr–40 hr) was a result of a continuous acceleration of the d-isomer (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The rise of d-/l-serine ratios at late time points (20 hr–40 hr) was a result of a continuous acceleration of the d-isomer.
source: The elevation of plasma d-/l-serine ratios at early time points (4 hr–8 hr) was due to a sharp decrease of the l-isomer, while the rise of d-/l-serine ratios at late time points (20 hr–40 hr) was a result of a continuous acceleration of the d-isomer (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The results of plasma d-serine were consistent with previous observations.

evidence: This is a statement comparing current results to previous findings, supported by citation.

claim: d-alanine, d-proline, and d-methionine were detected in certain amounts in the plasma.

claim: The d-/l-enantiomeric ratios of alanine, proline, and methionine were uncorrelated to the pathological conditions.
source: However, their d-/l- enantiomeric ratios were uncorrelated to the pathological conditions (Figure 1A).

claim: Alanine, serine, and proline share the same transport systems according to traditional amino acid transport knowledge.

source: The noticeably different profile of plasma d- and l-serine from those of alanine and proline led to the speculation that d-serine transport was possibly mediated by unique transport systems, different from those of d-alanine, d-proline, and the l-isomers.

claim: The unique d-serine transport systems would be sensitive to IRI conditions.
source: Notably, such transport systems would be sensitive to the IRI conditions.

claim: The ratios of urinary d-/l-serine were drastically decreased at early IRI (4 hr–8 hr).

claim: Similar tendencies of d-/l-amino acid ratios were observed in alanine, proline, asparagine, and histidine in urine.

claim: Urinary amino acid profiles indicated the impairment in both d- and l-amino acid reabsorption since the early injury.

claim: 4423 proteins were identified in the BBMV proteomics analysis.

claim: Ngal (Lcn2) showed a significant increase in the IRI model (4 hr IRI/sham = 1.8 folds; 8 hr IRI/sham = 9.5 folds).

claim: Ccn1 and Ngal are well-known early AKI biomarkers.

claim: The finding of increased Ccn1 and Ngal confirmed the reliability of the proteomics for molecular analysis of early AKI.

claim: 398 membrane transport proteins (325 transporters and 73 ion channels) were detected in the proteome.

claim: The decrease in transport of all micromolecules was due to the dramatic reduction of transport systems for heavy metals and organic compounds.
source: This decrease was due to the dramatic reduction of transport systems for heavy metals and organic compounds (Figure 2A).

evidence: This is a finding from the immunofluorescence staining experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 3B and citations.

claim: Asct2 did not co-localize with Na+/K+-ATPase, a basolateral membrane marker.

claim: Asct2 is localized at the apical side in all segments of proximal tubules.

claim: d-serine transport in SMCT1-PL was inhibited by ibuprofen, confirming SMCT1-mediated d-serine transport.

claim: Serine is the substrate of SMCT1 and the recognition is more stereoselective for the d- than the l-isomer.

claim: ASCT2 is an antiporter that influxes one amino acid with efflux of another.

claim: SMCTs are symporters.
source: ASCT2 is an antiporter, influx one amino acid with efflux of another, while SMCTs are symporters (Ganapathy et al., 2008; Scalise et al., 2018).
